claim: Blinks occlude the pupil for a considerable amount of time, typically 100–150 ms.
source: blinks occlude the pupil for a considerable amount of time, typically 100–150 ms (Riggs et al., 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Riggs et al., 1981.

claim: External darkenings of 100-150 ms duration cause a robust percept.
source: External darkenings of such duration have been shown to cause a robust percept (Riggs et al., 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Riggs et al., 1981.

claim: Blinks normally occur at least 1000 times an hour.
source: since blinks normally occur at least 1000 times an hour (Cruz et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cruz et al., 2011.

claim: About three or four percent of our waking hours are unknowingly spent with our eyes closed due to blinks.
source: about three or four percent of our waking hours are unknowingly spent with our eyes closed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the frequency and duration of blinks mentioned in the text.

claim: Spontaneous blinks are invisible.
source: While spontaneous blinks are invisible, voluntary blinks are not.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Voluntary blinks are not invisible but are experienced as shorter and less dim than physically comparable artificial darkenings.
source: However, their perception is also not veridical: they are experienced as shorter and less dim than physically comparable artificial darkenings (Riggs et al., 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Riggs et al., 1981.

claim: There is evidence for a decrease in visual sensitivity during blinks even when the optical-retinal impact of blinks was neutralized.
source: Human psychophysical experiments have found evidence for a decrease in visual sensitivity during blinks even when the optical-retinal impact of blinks was neutralized (Volkmann et al., 1980).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Volkmann et al., 1980.

claim: Blink-related decrease in visual sensitivity could be mediated by an extra-retinal suppression of the neural response in early visual cortices during blinks.
source: This effect could be mediated by an extra-retinal suppression of the neural response in early visual cortices during blinks, as indicated by feline V1 single unit recordings (Buisseret and Maffei, 1983) and human fMRI (Bristow et al., 2005b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Buisseret and Maffei, 1983 and Bristow et al., 2005b.

claim: Fourteen patients undergoing electrocorticographic evaluation for intractable epilepsy participated in the study.
source: Fourteen patients undergoing electrocorticographic evaluation for intractable epilepsy participated in the study (see Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study participants.

claim: The mean hit-rate for animal detection was 86.1%.
source: The patients clicked the mouse button each time they detected an animal image (mean hit-rate = 86.1%, mean false-alarm rate = 3.4%).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: The mean false-alarm rate for animal detection was 3.4%.
source: The patients clicked the mouse button each time they detected an animal image (mean hit-rate = 86.1%, mean false-alarm rate = 3.4%).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: In early visual areas (V1 and V2), the disappearance of the stimulus due to either invisible blinks or salient blank video frames ('gaps') led to a similar drop in activity level.
source: In early visual areas (V1 and V2), the disappearance of the stimulus due to either invisible blinks or salient blank video frames ('gaps') led to a similar drop in activity level, followed by a positive overshoot beyond baseline, triggered by stimulus reappearance.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by data presented in the results.

claim: In early visual areas (V1 and V2), stimulus disappearance due to blinks or gaps was followed by a positive overshoot beyond baseline, triggered by stimulus reappearance.
source: In early visual areas (V1 and V2), the disappearance of the stimulus due to either invisible blinks or salient blank video frames ('gaps') led to a similar drop in activity level, followed by a positive overshoot beyond baseline, triggered by stimulus reappearance.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by data presented in the results.

claim: Ascending the visual hierarchy, the reappearance-related overshoot gradually subsided for blinks but not for gaps.
source: Ascending the visual hierarchy, the reappearance-related overshoot gradually subsided for blinks but not for gaps.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by data presented in the results.

claim: The disappearance-related drop did not follow the perceptual distinction between blinks and gaps.
source: By contrast, the disappearance-related drop did not follow the perceptual distinction – it was actually slightly more pronounced for blinks than for gaps.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by data presented in the results.

claim: The disappearance-related drop was actually slightly more pronounced for blinks than for gaps.
source: By contrast, the disappearance-related drop did not follow the perceptual distinction – it was actually slightly more pronounced for blinks than for gaps.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by data presented in the results.

claim: Blinks' limited visibility compared with gaps is correlated with suppression of blink-related visual activity transients, rather than with 'filling-in' of the occluded content during blinks.
source: These findings suggest that blinks' limited visibility compared with gaps is correlated with suppression of blink-related visual activity transients, rather than with "filling-in" of the occluded content during blinks.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: 143 electrodes out of a total of 1585 were found to show visual responses that were both significant and of a considerable effect size.
source: 143 Electrodes out of a total of 1585 were found to show visual responses that were both significant (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.05, Bonferroni-corrected within-patient across electrodes) and of a considerable effect size (Glass' Δ ≥ 2, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct report of the data analysis results.

claim: 19 electrodes were identified as face-selective, found in 10 of the 14 patients.
source: This analysis identified 19 electrodes (found in 10 of the 14 patients, see Table 1) that responded significantly more strongly to faces than to any other category (Wilcoxon rank sum test, p<0.05 for all contrasts, uncorrected), located mostly in high-level ventral visual cortex.
evidence: This is a direct report of the data analysis results.

claim: Face-selective electrodes were located mostly in high-level ventral visual cortex.
source: This analysis identified 19 electrodes (found in 10 of the 14 patients, see Table 1) that responded significantly more strongly to faces than to any other category (Wilcoxon rank sum test, p<0.05 for all contrasts, uncorrected), located mostly in high-level ventral visual cortex.
evidence: This is a direct report of the anatomical location of the identified electrodes.

claim: In patient P46, both early visual sites (V1) and high-level ventral sites (Ventral Occipital) showed activity strongly modulated by blinks.
source: In both patient P46 (Figure 4a) and patient P39 (Figure 4b) there were concurrent recordings of ventral early (V1 and V2, respectively, defined by a surface-based probabilistic atlas, Wang et al., 2014) and ventral high-level (Ventral Occipital and Fusiform gyrus) visual sites. In both cases, activity in early visual sites was strongly modulated by blinks, undergoing a dip in activation levels following eye closure and then overshooting beyond expected activation levels as the eyes re-opened and the visual image reappeared.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: In patient P46, activity in early visual sites underwent a dip in activation levels following eye closure and then overshot beyond expected activation levels as the eyes re-opened.
source: In both cases, activity in early visual sites was strongly modulated by blinks, undergoing a dip in activation levels following eye closure and then overshooting beyond expected activation levels as the eyes re-opened and the visual image reappeared.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Gaps induced a qualitatively comparable effect to blinks in early visual sites – a negative dip in response to the onset of the display of the blank screen followed by a positive overshoot triggered by the reappearance of the stimulus.
source: Gaps induced a qualitatively comparable effect – a negative dip in response to the onset of the display of the blank screen followed by a positive overshoot triggered by the reappearance of the stimulus.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The two higher-level ventral electrodes in patients P46 and P39 showed considerable reappearance-related responses following the gaps, but largely no such responses to blinks.
source: By contrast, the two higher-level ventral electrodes showed considerable reappearance-related responses following the gaps, but largely, no such responses to blinks.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In patient P39, the high-level electrode was face-selective.
source: In P39, the high-level electrode was face-selective; by estimating blink and gap-related responses separately for face and non-face trials, we found that the reappearance-related overshoot induced by gaps (and to a lesser extent by voluntary blinks) in this electrode was face-selective as well.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: In patient P39, the reappearance-related overshoot induced by gaps in the high-level electrode was face-selective.
source: In P39, the high-level electrode was face-selective; by estimating blink and gap-related responses separately for face and non-face trials, we found that the reappearance-related overshoot induced by gaps (and to a lesser extent by voluntary blinks) in this electrode was face-selective as well.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: 51 sites out of 143 showed a significant advantage for gaps over spontaneous blinks in reappearance-related overshoot responses.
source: 51 sites (out of 143) showed a significant advantage for gaps over spontaneous blinks (two-tailed permutation test, pFDR < 0.05).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: The effect of gaps showing greater reappearance-related overshoot than spontaneous blinks was not uniformly distributed across the ROIs.
source: The effect was not uniformly distributed across the ROIs: V1 showed no significant electrodes out of 17 electrodes, V2 – 0/12, V3 – 5/15, V4 – 2/7, VO – 4/8, face-selective – 10/19 and high-level face non-selective ROI – 18/30. Randomization test of independence confirmed the apparent inhomogeneity of effect occurrence (χ2(6) = 17.219, p=0.00001).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: V1 showed no significant electrodes with greater reappearance-related overshoot for gaps over spontaneous blinks out of 17 electrodes.
source: V1 showed no significant electrodes out of 17 electrodes
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: V2 showed no significant electrodes with greater reappearance-related overshoot for gaps over spontaneous blinks out of 12 electrodes.
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: V3 showed 5 significant electrodes with greater reappearance-related overshoot for gaps over spontaneous blinks out of 15 electrodes.
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: V4 showed 2 significant electrodes with greater reappearance-related overshoot for gaps over spontaneous blinks out of 7 electrodes.
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: VO showed 4 significant electrodes with greater reappearance-related overshoot for gaps over spontaneous blinks out of 8 electrodes.
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: Face-selective ROI showed 10 significant electrodes with greater reappearance-related overshoot for gaps over spontaneous blinks out of 19 electrodes.
source: face-selective – 10/19
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: High-level face non-selective ROI showed 18 significant electrodes with greater reappearance-related overshoot for gaps over spontaneous blinks out of 30 electrodes.
source: high-level face non-selective ROI – 18/30
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: 35 of 108 electrodes showed significant advantage of gaps over voluntary blinks in reappearance-related overshoot.
source: Comparing voluntary blinks with gaps (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) revealed a similar, but weaker pattern: 35 of 108 electrodes recorded in the 10 patients who performed voluntary blinks showed significant advantage of gaps over voluntary blinks (two-tailed permutation test, pFDR < 0.05)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: No electrodes showed significantly greater reappearance-related overshoot for voluntary blinks than for gaps.
source: No electrodes showed significantly greater reappearance-related overshoot for voluntary blinks than for gaps.
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: No electrode showed significantly greater dips for gaps than for spontaneous blinks.
source: No electrode showed significantly greater dips for gaps than for spontaneous blinks, again a result inconsistent with the selective filling-in hypothesis.
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results.

claim: The interaction of ROI with interruption type was significant for reappearance-related overshoot (F(12,471.29) = 4.38, p<0.001).
source: The two ANOVA tests of primary interest are (a) the interaction of ROI with interruption, which was significant (F(12,471.29) = 4.38, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the mixed-effects model.

claim: The three-way interaction between ROI, interruption and category was not significant for reappearance-related overshoot (F(12,463.31) = 0.59, p=0.85).
source: the three-way interaction between ROI, interruption and category, which was not significant (F(12,463.31) = 0.59, p=0.85)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the mixed-effects model.

claim: In face-trials, gaps showed significantly larger reappearance-related overshoot responses compared with voluntary blinks in VO, the face-selective and high-level face non-selective ROIs (pFDR < 0.05).
source: In agreement with our previous analysis, in face-trials, gaps showed significantly larger reappearance-related overshoot responses compared with voluntary blinks both in VO, the face-selective and high-level face non-selective ROIs (pFDR < 0.05).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the mixed-effects model.

claim: Compared with spontaneous blinks, gaps had significantly larger reappearance-related overshoot response in V3 in face-trials (pFDR < 0.05).
source: Compared with spontaneous blinks, gaps had significantly larger reappearance-related overshoot response also in V3 (pFDR < 0.05).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the mixed-effects model.

claim: In non-face trials, gaps had a significantly larger overshoot response compared with voluntary blinks in the high-level face non-selective ROI.
source: In non-face trials (Figure 7b), gaps had a significantly larger overshoot response compared with voluntary blinks in the high-level face non-selective ROI.
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the mixed-effects model.

claim: Compared with spontaneous blinks, gaps had significantly larger reappearance-related overshoot in non-face trials in V3 and VO.
source: Compared with spontaneous blinks, gaps had significantly larger reappearance-related overshoot (in non-face trials) also in V3 and VO.
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the mixed-effects model.

claim: The interaction of ROI and interruption was significant for disappearance-related activation-dip (F(12,466.48) = 4.26, p<0.001).
source: Fitting the disappearance-related activation-dip component with the same mixed-effects model (Figure 7c–d) also found a significant interaction of ROI and interruption (F(12,466.48) = 4.26, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the mixed-effects model.

claim: The three-way interaction of interruption, category and ROI was not significant for disappearance-related activation-dip (F(12,463.10) = 0.45, p=0.94).
source: As in the reappearance-related overshoot data, the three-way interaction of interruption, category and ROI was not significant (F(12,463.10) = 0.45, p=0.94).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the mixed-effects model.

claim: The activation dip triggered by gaps was smaller compared to that triggered by voluntary blinks in most ROIs (pFDR < 0.05).
source: Inspecting the effects between the three kinds of interruptions within each ROI found that the activation dip triggered by gaps was smaller (more shallow) compared to that triggered by voluntary blinks in most ROIs (see Figure 7c–d for detailed simple effects results, pFDR < 0.05)
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the mixed-effects model.

claim: The activation dip triggered by gaps was smaller than the dip triggered by spontaneous blinks in V1 and V2 (both face and non-face trials, pFDR < 0.05).
source: it was also smaller than the dip triggered by spontaneous blinks in V1 and V2 (both face and non-face trials, pFDR < 0.05).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the mixed-effects model.

claim: No evidence was observed for greater (deeper) activation dip for gaps compared with either spontaneous or voluntary blinks in any ROI.
source: Importantly, no evidence was observed for greater (deeper) activation dip for gaps compared with either spontaneous or voluntary blinks in any ROI
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis results from the mixed-effects model.

claim: The striking similarity in the response profile of early visual electrodes between the spontaneous blinks and the gaps reinforces single-unit results from non-human primates comparing reflex-blinks with external darkenings.
source: The striking similarity in the response profile of early visual electrodes between the spontaneous blinks and the gaps, despite their marked perceptual difference, reinforces single-unit results from non-human primates comparing reflex-blinks with external darkenings (Gawne and Martin, 2000, 2002)
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current findings in the context of previous research cited.

claim: Early visual responses are driven mainly by the optical stimuli impinging on the retina and are minimally related to their perceptual status, when the low-level inputs are similar.
source: strongly supports the notion that early visual responses are driven mainly by the optical stimuli impinging on the retina and are minimally related to their perceptual status, when the low-level inputs are similar.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current findings in the context of previous research.

claim: Individuals with early visual cortex lesions report vivid visual experiences during dreaming.
source: including individuals with early visual cortex lesions that nevertheless report vivid visual experiences during dreaming (Solms, 1997)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Solms, 1997.

claim: Individuals with early visual cortex lesions report vivid visual experiences even while awake.
source: or even while awake (Ashwin and Tsaloumas, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ashwin and Tsaloumas, 2007.

claim: Bursts of high-frequency broadband activity in ventral higher-level cortex are correlated with the appearance of perceived visual object images.
source: This result reinforces the ecological validity of the view that bursts of high-frequency broadband activity in ventral higher-level cortex are correlated with the appearance of perceived visual object images, previously demonstrated using backward-masked near-threshold stimuli (Fisch et al., 2009; Moutard et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current findings in the context of previous research cited.

claim: Voluntary blinks are visible but systematically underperceived.
source: This may reflect the intermediate perceptual status of voluntary blinks, visible but systematically underperceived (Riggs et al., 1981).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Riggs et al., 1981.

claim: The most likely interpretation of the reduction in blink-related transients in higher-level visual cortex is extra-retinal suppression of the cortical neural response to the retinal impact of blinks.
source: Given the evidence from the early visual cortex of a similar retinal impact of blinks and gaps, the most likely (but not exclusive, see below) interpretation of the reduction in blink-related transients in higher-level visual cortex is extra-retinal suppression of the cortical neural response to the retinal impact of blinks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings based on the data and logical reasoning.

claim: Studies neutralizing blinks' retinal impact have demonstrated a certain degree of extra-retinal blink-related effects already in V1.
source: Whereas studies neutralizing blinks' retinal impact have demonstrated a certain degree of extra-retinal blink-related effects already in V1 (Buisseret and Maffei, 1983; Bristow et al., 2005b)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Buisseret and Maffei, 1983 and Bristow et al., 2005b.

claim: The effective locus of the suppression of neural responses to blinks is likely further up the visual hierarchy than V1.
source: our results suggest that the effective locus of the suppression of neural responses to blinks is likely further up the visual hierarchy.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the current findings.

claim: Differences between the responses to blinks and external darkenings observed in a small minority of early visual cortex single units in the macaque may act as precursors to the differential reappearance-related response at the population level observed in human higher-level visual cortex.
source: It may be that the differences between the responses to blinks and external darkenings that were observed in a small minority of early visual cortex single units in the macaque (Gawne and Martin, 2000, 2002) may act as precursors to the differential reappearance-related response at the population level we observed in human higher-level visual cortex.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation connecting previous findings with the current results.

claim: An obvious candidate for a blink-suppressing signal is 'corollary discharge' or 'efference copy' – a copy of the motor command to execute the blink that is sent in parallel to the visual cortex, via a motor-sensory pathway.
source: An obvious candidate of such a signal is that of 'corollary discharge' or 'efference copy' – a copy of the motor command to execute the blink that is sent in parallel to the visual cortex, via a motor-sensory pathway (see Wurtz, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation to Wurtz, 2013.

claim: The motor-sensory pathway for blink suppression might be shared with saccades.
source: This pathway might be shared with saccades: this possibility is supported by psychophysical similarities of blink-suppression and saccade-suppression (Bidder and Tomlinson, 1997) and by the documented occurrence of a brief 1–2° rotation of the eye during the downward phase of the blink, which might provide a sufficient efferent signal to enable blink suppression (Riggs et al., 1987).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to Bidder and Tomlinson, 1997 and Riggs et al., 1987.

claim: Neural activity that reliably preceded the execution of blinks was not detected in any of the recording sites.
source: The potential source of the suppressing signal was not observed in the current study: neural activity that reliably preceded the execution of blinks was not detected in any of our recording sites.
evidence: This is a direct statement about what was not observed in the data.

claim: The lack of detection of neural activity preceding blinks might be related to incomplete coverage of oculomotor cortical regions.
source: This might be related either to our incomplete coverage of oculomotor cortical regions or to the potential sub-cortical locus of the (spontaneous) blink generator (Kaminer et al., 2011), which was obviously not covered by our recordings.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of why the signal was not detected, supported by a citation to Kaminer et al., 2011.

claim: The lack of detection of neural activity preceding blinks might be related to the potential sub-cortical locus of the spontaneous blink generator.
source: This might be related either to our incomplete coverage of oculomotor cortical regions or to the potential sub-cortical locus of the (spontaneous) blink generator (Kaminer et al., 2011), which was obviously not covered by our recordings.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of why the signal was not detected, supported by a citation to Kaminer et al., 2011.

claim: The discounting of responses to blinks might be achieved by a more general-purpose prediction error minimizing mechanism.
source: An alternative possibility to efference copy is that the discounting of responses to blinks is achieved by a more general-purpose prediction error minimizing mechanism (e.g. Bastos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative alternative interpretation supported by a citation to Bastos et al., 2012.

claim: Neural adaptation may be involved in the observed reduction of blink-related transients.
source: An additional potential factor that may be involved in the observed reduction of blink-related transients is neural adaptation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of a potential mechanism.

claim: A plausible neural mechanism that may underlie continuity of neural activity could be the self-reverberatory dynamics in ventral high-order regions that lead to a sluggish all-or none response.
source: A plausible neural mechanism that may underlie such continuity of neural activity could be the self-reverberatory dynamics in ventral high-order regions that lead to a sluggish all-or none response (Fisch et al., 2009; Moutard et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to Fisch et al., 2009 and Moutard et al., 2015.

claim: There is a consistent and rapid decline in the HFB activity in high-order visual areas during the one-second long display of the stimulus.
source: Additional evidence for a dissociation between momentary activity reductions and perceptual disappearance in high-order visual areas can be found in the consistent and rapid decline we observed in the HFB activity in these regions during the one-second long display of the stimulus (Figure 5b), an effect with no apparent perceptual correlate.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The rapid decline in HFB activity during stimulus display has no apparent perceptual correlate.
source: the consistent and rapid decline we observed in the HFB activity in these regions during the one-second long display of the stimulus (Figure 5b), an effect with no apparent perceptual correlate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Signal reduction on its own may simply fail to register perceptually in high-order visual areas.
source: Thus, it is interesting to note that the occurrence of signal decline without perceptual disappearance (Figure 5b) and perceptual disappearance (gap) without signal decline (Figure 5a) complement each other in suggesting that signal reduction on its own may simply fail to register perceptually.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data shown in Figures 5a and 5b.

claim: The perceptually-relevant signals, at least in high-order visual areas, may be phasic bursts rather than continuous activations.
source: It is tempting to speculate based on these converging phenomena that perhaps the perceptually-relevant signals, at least in high-order visual areas, are phasic bursts rather continuous activations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data.

claim: The perception of brief stimulus disappearance may be reliably represented by a positive signal.
source: One possibility is that the perception of brief stimulus disappearance may be reliably represented by a positive signal.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: A burst of activity in higher-level dorsal stream sites may underlie the percept of a flicker caused by a stimulus disappearance (gap) or external darkening.
source: It is conceivable that the onset (disappearance-related) and offset (reappearance-related) sensitive responses in higher-level dorsal stream sites that we noted (albeit infrequently due to coverage limitations. See Figure 4—figure supplement 1) play a critical role in this task: a burst of activity in such sites may underlie the percept of a flicker caused by a stimulus disappearance (gap) or external darkening.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: During blinks, blink-suppression signals may actively block detectors of discontinuity, resulting in the experience of continuously perceived stimuli.
source: By contrast, during blinks, blink-suppression signals may actively block these detectors of discontinuity, resulting in the experience of continuously perceived stimuli (Figure 8b).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation illustrated in Figure 8b.

claim: The neuronal representation of perceived face-disappearance is found outside the ventral face-selective areas.
source: Thus, we propose that the neuronal representation of perceived face-disappearance is found outside the ventral face-selective areas.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation based on the findings.

claim: One cannot attribute the content of a conscious percept to a single cortical element, necessitating a joint-representation across diverse content-selective regions.
source: The upshot of this is that one cannot attribute the content of a conscious percept to a single cortical element, necessitating a joint-representation across diverse content-selective regions.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: All patients gave fully informed consent, including consent to publish, according to NIH guidelines.
source: All patients gave fully informed consent, including consent to publish, according to NIH guidelines, as monitored by the institutional review board at the Feinstein Institute for Medical Research, in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: This is a statement about the ethical procedures followed in the study.

claim: Data was obtained as part of protocol number 07–125.
source: Data was obtained as part of protocol number 07–125.
evidence: This is a statement about the ethical procedures followed in the study.

claim: Five additional patients performed the experiment but their recordings were excluded after initial data quality inspection.
source: Five additional patients performed the experiment but their recordings were excluded after initial data quality inspection.
evidence: This is a statement about the data collection and exclusion criteria.

claim: Reasons for exclusion of five patients were independent of the main analyses and consisted of: (1) widespread interictal spikes, (2) no visual coverage, (3) severe visual field impairments (4) contamination of the ECoG signal by synchronization triggers and (5) a case in which the patient misunderstood the instructions to voluntary blink and executed prolonged eye closures (mean duration of 642 ms) instead.
source: Reasons for exclusion were independent of the main analyses and consisted of: (1) widespread interictal spikes, (2) no visual coverage, (3) severe visual field impairments (4) contamination of the ECoG signal by synchronization triggers and (5) a case in which the patient misunderstood the instructions to voluntary blink and executed prolonged eye closures (mean duration of 642 ms) instead.
evidence: This is a statement about the data collection and exclusion criteria.

claim: The subjects were seated in bed in front of an LCD monitor, approximately 70 cm from the screen.
source: The subjects were seated in bed in front of an LCD monitor, approximately 70 cm from the screen.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: The images subtended a visual angle of 15.8°.
source: The images subtended a visual angle of 15.8°.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: A total of 32 blocks per subject were considered for this study.
source: A total of 32 blocks per subject were considered for this study
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In 10 of the 14 patients, twelve of the blocks were preceded by an auditory cue to blink at a steady pace of one blink per second until a stop signal that followed the block's end.
source: In 10 of the 14 patients (see Table 1), twelve of the blocks were preceded by an auditory cue to blink at a steady pace of one blink per second until a stop signal that followed the block's end.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In the rest of the blocks, gaps in the visual stimulation were pseudo-randomly introduced in 60% of the trials at 350, 550 or 750 ms post stimulus transition.
source: In the rest of the blocks, gaps in the visual stimulation were pseudo-randomly introduced in 60% of the trials at 350, 550 or 750 ms post stimulus transition.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: A wide range of gap durations (100–200 ms in most patients) was applied in order to allow for post-hoc matching of blinks and gaps.
source: We applied a wide range of gap durations (100–200 ms in most patients, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1) in order to allow for post-hoc matching of blinks and gaps.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design rationale.

claim: Each patient participated in a single session that was divided by three short breaks in which the patients were required to rest with their eyes closed.
source: Each patient participated in a single session that was divided by three short breaks in which the patients were required to rest with their eyes closed.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Including the breaks, an entire session typically lasted about 15 min.
source: Including the breaks, an entire session typically lasted about 15 min.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: In nine of the subjects (starting at P36), half of the gaps were gray (intensity level 183/255) instead of black (0/255 intensity level).
source: In nine of the subjects (starting at P36), half of the gaps were gray (intensity level 183/255, where the object stimuli mean intensity level was 160/255) instead of black (0/255 intensity level)
